entry: French lawyer and statesman, a radical Jacobin leader of the [[French Revolution]]. Elected a deputy to the National Convention in September 1792, Robespierre joined the Committee of Public Safety in July 1793 and became its leading figure. He campaigned for voting rights for all men, the right to petition and the abolition of the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. He defended the [[Reign of Terror]] as an instrument of justice, a period that saw at least 17,000 official executions by [[Guillotine|guillotine]]. Growing accusations of excess turned the Convention against him, and after his arrest on 9 Thermidor he was executed without trial. His legacy remains contested: critics stress his role in repressing the Revolution's opponents, while others note his progressive views for the time.

[[Probability distribution]] of particle speeds in an idealized gas at thermal equilibrium. Named after [[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[Ludwig Boltzmann]], it was first derived by Maxwell in 1860 on heuristic grounds, and Boltzmann later investigated its physical origins in the 1870s. Mathematically, it is a chi distribution with three degrees of freedom, with a scale parameter proportional to the square root of T/m, the ratio of temperature to particle mass. The distribution underlies the kinetic theory of gases, which explains properties such as [[Pressure|pressure]] and [[Diffusion|diffusion]]. It is an excellent approximation for rarefied gases at ordinary temperatures and for ideal plasmas.

Thought experiment of 1867 devised by [[James Clerk Maxwell]]. A demon controls a door between two gas-filled chambers, letting only fast-moving molecules pass one way and slow-moving ones the other. One chamber warms and the other cools, decreasing entropy without any work and seemingly violating the [[Second law of thermodynamics|second law of thermodynamics]]. Maxwell called the agent a "finite being"; [[Lord Kelvin]] later named it a "demon." The idea stimulated work on the relationship between thermodynamics and [[Information theory]]. Most scientists argue that no device can violate the second law in this way, and experimental versions differ from the original; none has been shown to violate it.

Set of coupled [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] describing [[Electromagnetism|classical electromagnetism]]. Together with the [[Lorentz force|Lorentz force law]], they describe how [[Electric field|electric]] and [[Magnetic field|magnetic fields]] are generated by electric charges and currents, and they form the foundation of classical optics and of electric and magnetic circuits. They underpin technologies from power generation and electric motors to wireless communication and radar. An early form was published by James Clerk Maxwell in 1861 and 1862, and the modern form is credited to Oliver Heaviside. Since the mid-20th century the equations have been understood as a classical limit of [[Quantum electrodynamics]]. Their covariant formulation makes compatibility with [[Special relativity]] apparent, and they are compatible with [[General relativity]] in curved spacetime.

Fifth month of the year in the [[Julian calendar|Julian]] and [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian]] calendars, with 31 days. It is a spring month in the Northern Hemisphere and an autumn month in the Southern Hemisphere. The name was taken from the Greek goddess Maia, who was identified with the Roman goddess of fertility, Bona Dea; the Roman poet Ovid gave a second etymology, from the maiores, Latin for "elders." The birthstone is the emerald. The zodiac signs are Taurus until May 20 and Gemini from May 21.

Period of protests, riots and strikes in [[France]] beginning in May 1968. Sparked by student demonstrations against university conditions and government repression, it escalated into the largest general strike in French history, involving about 10 million workers. Factories, transportation and public services shut down, and on May 27 the Grenelle agreements brought wage increases and concessions. [[Charles de Gaulle|President Charles de Gaulle]] briefly left for a French military base in West Germany on May 29, then dissolved the National Assembly. His party won a resounding victory in the June elections, and the movement lost momentum. De Gaulle resigned the following year.

American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist. She published seven autobiographies, three books of essays and several poetry collections. Her memoir *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings* (1969), covering her life to age 17, brought her international recognition. Born Marguerite Annie Johnson in St. Louis, Missouri, she worked with [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] and [[Malcolm X]] in the [[Civil rights movement]]. In 1993 she recited her poem *On the Pulse of Morning* at the first inauguration of [[Bill Clinton]], the first poet to give an inaugural recitation since [[Robert Frost]] at [[John F. Kennedy]]'s inauguration in 1961. Her works, which address racism, identity and family, are widely taught, though attempts have been made to ban them from some U.S. libraries.

Ethnolinguistic group of Indigenous peoples of [[Mesoamerica]], generally descended from the populations of the ancient [[Maya civilization]]. An estimated seven million Maya lived in the region at the start of the 21st century, mainly in [[Guatemala]], southeastern [[Mexico]], Belize, and western [[El Salvador]] and [[Honduras]]. "Maya" is a modern collective term that the peoples did not historically use themselves, and there was no common political identity among them. The largest group, the Yucatec Maya, lives on the [[Yucatán Peninsula]]. The Yucatán was first contacted by Europeans after Spanish shipwreck survivors came ashore in 1511, and [[Chichen Itza]] was conquered by 1570.

Traditional religion of the [[Maya peoples|Maya]] of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras and parts of Mexico, part of the wider [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerican]] religion. Including its pre-Hispanic antecedents, it has existed as a distinct phenomenon for more than two and a half millennia, spread across many indigenous kingdoms with their own local traditions. It resulted from centuries of symbiosis with Roman Catholicism and coexists with [[Syncretism|syncretism]] promoted by the Pan-Maya movement and with Christianity. Ritual is central: landmarks such as mountains, wells and caves are assigned to ancestors and deities, and [[Cenote|cenotes]] in Yucatán are sites of ritual activity. Key sources include the surviving codices of Dresden, Madrid and Paris and the early colonial [[Popol Vuh]].

Writing system of the [[Maya civilization]], the only Mesoamerican script that has been substantially deciphered. The earliest identifiable Maya inscriptions date to the 3rd century BCE in late Preclassic sites such as San Bartolo in Guatemala. Writing continued until the Spanish conquest of the 16th and 17th centuries, though knowledge of it was reserved to the elite. Maya script combined [[Logogram|logograms]] with syllabic glyphs, somewhat like modern Japanese writing, and recorded Classic Maya and, in northern Yucatán, Yucatec Maya. Texts were written in blocks arranged in columns two blocks wide. Early European explorers called it hieroglyphics, though it is unrelated to [[Egyptian hieroglyphs]]. As of 2008, the sound of about 80% of the writing could be read and the meaning of about 60% understood with varying certainty.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in Albay province on [[Luzon]], Philippines. Renowned for its symmetric "perfect cone" and regarded as sacred in Philippine mythology, it rises 2,463 m (8,081 ft) from the shores of Albay Gulf. It was declared a national park on July 20, 1938, the first in the nation, and is the centerpiece of the Albay Biosphere Reserve, declared by UNESCO in 2016. It is the most active volcano in the Philippines, monitored by the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology. At least 85 lava flows have been identified, and it forms part of the Pacific [[Ring of Fire]].

Thick, creamy [[Sauce|sauce]], an [[Emulsion|emulsion]] of oil, egg yolk and vinegar or lemon juice. It is commonly used on sandwiches, [[Hamburger|hamburgers]], [[Salad|salads]] and [[French fries]], and forms the base for tartar sauce, remoulade and ranch dressing. Its origin is debated, but most hypotheses place it in Mahón on Menorca, where French troops were stationed during the [[Seven Years' War]]; the Duke of Richelieu took the port on April 18, 1756. The term appeared in French in 1806, and Antonin Carême described a cold emulsified version with egg yolk in 1815. Commercial production emerged in the early 20th century, and eggless versions are available for those who avoid eggs.

Overseas department and region of France (pop., 2024: 320,901) in the northern [[Mozambique Channel]], western Indian Ocean. Its land area is 374 sq km, and its largest city and prefecture, Mamoudzou, lies on the main island, Grande-Terre. French is the official language; the native languages are Shimaore and Kibushi, a [[Malagasy language]]. A sultanate was established in 1500, and most residents are Muslim. Sold to France in 1841, Mayotte chose to remain French when the nearby [[Comoros]] became independent in 1974. It became France's 101st department on March 31, 2011, and an outermost region of the European Union in 2014. Illegal immigration from the Comoros is a major political issue, and a 2018 INSEE report found that over 83% of the population lived below the poverty line by French standards.

Japanese multinational automotive manufacturer, headquartered in Fuchū, [[Hiroshima]]. Founded in 1920 as Toyo Cork Kogyo, a cork factory, it began producing vehicles in 1931 with the Mazda-Go auto rickshaw. The company is known for the [[Wankel engine]], the SkyActiv platform and its Kodo design language, and it won the [[24 Hours of Le Mans]] in 1991 with the rotary-powered Mazda 787B. [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] was a major shareholder from 1974 until the late 2000s. In 2023 it produced 1.1 million vehicles globally.

Path or collection of paths, typically from an entrance to a goal, used as a puzzle or as a garden feature. Mazes may be built from hedges, turf, walls or corn stalks, and [[Maize|maize]] mazes are often promoted as seasonal tourist attractions. Mazes without loops are called perfect mazes and are equivalent to a tree in [[Graph theory]]. [[Leonhard Euler]] was one of the first to analyze plane mazes mathematically, making early contributions to [[Topology]]. Psychologists use mazes such as the Morris water maze and the T-maze to study spatial navigation, usually with [[Rat|rats]] or mice. The term "labyrinth" is generally synonymous, though it can connote a unicursal pattern without branches.

City and capital of Kasai-Oriental Province in the south-central [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], known until the end of 1962 as Bakwanga. It is thought to be the second-largest city in the country after [[Kinshasa]], though estimates of its population range from 1,480,000 (2010 CIA World Factbook) to 3,500,000 (UN, 2008). The name, from the Tshiluba language, means "Goat-Water." The city sits on one of the largest diamond deposits in the world and is the traditional center of industrial [[Diamond|diamond]] mining in Congo. Diamonds were discovered in the area as early as 1907, and in 1963 the local MIBA company was the source of 80 percent of the world's industrial diamonds.

Political practice of accusing left-wing Americans of communist and Soviet influence, prominent in the late 1940s and 1950s. Associated with Senator [[Joseph McCarthy]], it lost support after the mid-1950s, when several of his accusations proved false. Rulings of the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Earl Warren on civil and political rights helped end the Second Red Scare. Some historians since the 1980s argue that the term overstates McCarthy's role; Ellen Schrecker has suggested "Hooverism," after FBI head [[J. Edgar Hoover]]. Documents released after the [[Cold War]] revealed Soviet espionage in the United States, though many agents were never identified by McCarthy.

American multinational fast-food restaurant chain. Founded in 1940 as a restaurant in San Bernardino, California, by brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald, the company grew under [[Ray Kroc]], a franchise agent who opened a restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois, in 1955 and bought the brothers' stake in 1961. At the end of 2025 the system comprised 45,356 restaurants in more than 100 countries, approximately 95% of them operated by franchisees. Its menu centers on [[Hamburger|hamburgers]] and [[French fries]], including the Big Mac. It directly employed more than 150,000 people, and more than two million others worked at franchised restaurants. The chain has faced criticism over nutrition, treatment of animals, environmental impact and employee wages.

Twin-engine, single-aisle jet airliner designed by the Douglas Aircraft Company. The DC-9-10 first flew on February 25, 1965, and entered service with [[Delta Air Lines|Delta]] in December of that year. Powered by two rear-mounted [[Turbofan|turbofan]] engines under a T-tail, it could use 5,000-foot runways to serve smaller airports. Deliveries ended in October 1982, with 976 built. The MD-80 and MD-90 followed, and after the 1997 merger with [[Boeing]] the final version became the Boeing 717. The family had 2,441 deliveries between 1965 and 2006.

Twin-engine, all-weather fighter designed by McDonnell Douglas (now part of [[Boeing]]). The United States Air Force selected the design in 1969 as a dedicated air superiority fighter; it first flew in July 1972 and entered service in 1976. The Eagle is credited with over 104 victories and no losses in air-to-air combat. It was exported to Israel, Japan and [[Saudi Arabia]]. The Israeli Air Force first used it in combat in 1979, and it saw action in the [[Gulf War]] of 1991. Reduced procurement of the F-22 led the Air Force to keep F-15C/D fighters until 2030 and to supplement the F-22 with the F-15EX.

British motor racing team based in Woking, Surrey, [[England]]. Founded by Bruce McLaren in 1963, it is the second-oldest active [[Formula One]] team and the second-most successful after Ferrari, with 206 race wins, 13 Drivers' Championships and 10 Constructors' Championships. It is one of only three constructors, and the only team, to complete the Triple Crown of Motorsport, with wins at the Indianapolis 500, the [[24 Hours of Le Mans]] and the Monaco Grand Prix. A partnership with [[Honda]] from 1988 to 1991 produced four consecutive Constructors' Championships. The team's most recent titles were secured in 2025.

American Antarctic research station on the southern tip of Ross Island, the largest community on [[Antarctica]]. Run by the United States Antarctic Program, it supports up to 1,200 residents, fewer than 200 during the [[Polar night|polar night]]. It is one of three year-round United States Antarctic science facilities and the usual route to Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station. Sea ice can limit access to its seaport, Winter Quarters Bay, and its main airfields are built on ice. Established in the mid-1950s, it is powered by generators and wind power; it had a nuclear reactor in the 1960s. New Zealand's Scott Base is nearby.

Social movement against sexual abuse, sexual harassment and rape culture. The phrase "Me Too" was used on [[Myspace]] around 2006 by activist Tarana Burke. The hashtag #MeToo spread virally in October 2017 after allegations against film producer [[Harvey Weinstein]], and Facebook reported that almost half of its American users were friends with someone who said they had been sexually assaulted or harassed. Studies by the U.S. Department of Justice and the UK Home Office estimate that false reports make up only 2–10% of sexual assault claims, though some worry about false accusations. Critics argue that the movement overlooks police abuse and sex workers.

Open [[Habitat|habitat]] or field vegetated mainly by grasses, [[Herb|herbs]] and other non-woody plants. Meadows are usually semi-natural grasslands, often created by clearing shrub or woodland for [[Hay|hay]], fodder or livestock, and they support a wide range of wildlife, including pollinating insects. Intensive practices such as frequent mowing and mineral fertilizers reduce biodiversity. In the [[United Kingdom]] and [[Ireland]], "meadow" traditionally means a hay meadow mown in summer. Traditional hay meadows were once common in rural Britain, but England and Wales have lost about 97% of them over the past century. Deep-rooted grasses store substantial carbon in soil, making meadows potential carbon sinks.

Occasion at a specific time that involves the consumption of food, larger, more varied and more filling than a [[Snack|snack]]. Regular meals occur daily, typically several times a day, and usually take place at home or in restaurants. Special meals mark occasions such as [[Birthday|birthdays]], [[Wedding|weddings]], funerals and holidays. Three main meals are common in most civilizations, in the morning, early afternoon and evening, though names vary by region and family. The word [[Breakfast|breakfast]] refers literally to breaking the fast of the night. A full breakfast, popular in the United Kingdom and Ireland, usually includes bacon, sausages and eggs with hot drinks such as [[Coffee|coffee]] or tea.
